 Colombia’s 42-Hour Workweek Shapes the 2027 Minimum Wage Debate C 
 By jhoanbaron 
 -
 November 2, 2026 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 Colombia ’s 42-hour workweek adds pressure to 2027 minimum wage talks as employers and unions weigh costs and pay. 
 Colombia’s 42-hour workweek has become an important factor in the debate over the 2027 minimum wage because fewer working hours increase the cost of each hour for employers, even when monthly salaries stay the same. Since July 15, the country’s maximum workweek has stood at 42 hours, completing a gradual reduction from 48 hours that began in 2023 under a 2021 law. The legislation requires employers to maintain workers’ monthly salaries and benefits.
 Business groups argue, according to Valora Analitik, that the higher hourly cost and new adjustments to night, Sunday and holiday surcharges should limit the next minimum wage increase. Their argument rests on a straightforward calculation: when employers divide the same monthly salary across fewer working hours, each hour becomes more expensive before any new wage adjustment.
 Labor unions take a different position . They argue that workers have lost purchasing power over the years and want a substantial increase. Negotiations opening in the coming weeks will test how Colombia balances workers’ demands with employers’ rising labor costs. Understanding the impact of the shorter workweek helps explain why both sides are approaching the 2027 decision from different positions.
 How the 42-hour workweek raises hourly labor costs
 The change looks small on paper, but it affects payrolls across the country because it increases the cost of each hour worked. For a worker earning the 2026 minimum wage of 1,750,905 pesos (US$554), the ordinary hourly rate rose from 7,959 pesos to 8,338 pesos (US$2.52 to US$2.64) on July 15. That represents an increase of about 4.8% without any change in monthly salary.
 Overtime and surcharges are calculated using that same base rate, so a daytime overtime hour now costs about 10,400 pesos. A second change will take effect July 1, 2027, when the surcharge for working on Sundays and holidays climbs from 90% to 100% of the ordinary hourly rate. Consulting firm Crowe calculates that the additional pay per hour for a minimum-wage worker would rise from 7,504 pesos to about 9,005 pesos if the minimum wage increases by 8%.
 Many companies prepared in advance. A survey by the human resources association Acrip found that more than 71% were already working 44-hour weeks before July, while some had even moved to four-day schedules. Even so, businesses say the pressure adds to three or four years of rising labor costs, explaining why they are calling for a cautious increase as negotiations begin.

 How Colombia will decide the 2027 minimum wage
 The calendar for the decision is clear, even if the final figure is not. Employers, unions and the Government meet in a permanent commission to negotiate the minimum wage, with a Dec. 15 deadline to reach an agreement. If they fail, each side must explain its position, and the Government has until Dec. 30 to set the increase by decree. The new rate takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
 The proposals already show how far apart the sides stand. Unions have floated an increase of 38.5%, a figure their national coordinating body has not yet approved. Meanwhile, analyses cited by the press outline scenarios of 6.29% (the latest annual inflation rate ), 8% and 10%. These would put the minimum wage at approximately 1.86 million to 1.93 million pesos (US$588 to US$610), while the union proposal would bring it to about 2.4 million pesos (US$759).
 Colombia’s last increase was 23%, making the next decision more difficult: workers expect another substantial raise, while companies fear a further jump in costs. The shorter workweek adds another dimension, as employers weigh its effects on hiring, formal employment and prices, while unions argue that productivity gains should benefit workers. The December negotiations will determine how the country balances the effects of reduced working hours with wage demands and business costs in 2027.
